description: Independent English self-study aligned to CTFL syllabus v4.0.1: 24 practical lessons, every learning objective, 160 original questions and four distinct full mock papers. Includes 60- and 75-minute practice versions. Not official or accredited ISTQB material.

objectives.title: FL-1.2.3 · Errors, defects, failures and causes
FL-1.4.2 · Context and the test process

lessons.title: Start here · Your Foundation 4.0 preparation route
lessons.summary: Understand the exam, choose a study route and preserve fresh mock papers.

blocks.text: This independent English study pack is aligned to CTFL syllabus v4.0.1, the errata revision for Foundation 4.0. It is not an official exam or accredited training course. Start with the six chapters, work through the examples, then use untimed learning sessions to understand mistakes. All examinable learning objectives are linked to lessons and practice.

blocks.title: Exam format
blocks.text: The full simulation has 40 multiple-choice questions worth one point each, 60 minutes and a pass mark of 26. Select-N questions require exactly the stated number and award no partial credit. Extended-time practice uses 75 minutes; eligibility for an actual language allowance is determined by your exam provider.

blocks.title: A practical route
blocks.text: First pass: read the lessons and solve self-checks before revealing their solutions. Second pass: work on technique calculations and review terminology. Third pass: take paper A under timed conditions, review every uncertain answer, and repeat with B, C and D on separate days. A 20-question short session is a practice exercise, not a full exam.

blocks.title: Fresh evidence
blocks.text: The four papers contain different questions. Taking the 75-minute version of a paper repeats its questions. Learning practice also exposes questions from this bank. Preserve at least three unopened full papers if you want to meet the default readiness rule: strictly above 90% on each of three full mocks with 100% fresh families. A simulated pass is separate from that recommendation.

blocks.title: Sources and authorship
blocks.text: ISTQB and the authors named in its syllabus own the official syllabus and exam-rule documents. This pack contains original explanations, examples and questions; it does not reproduce official sample exams. The pack source list links to official materials and the glossary. K1 means recall, K2 means understanding, and K3 means applying a technique.

lessons.title: 1.1 · Testing and debugging
lessons.summary: Learn and practise testing and debugging.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Testing evaluates work products and provides information for decisions. Activities include reviewing requirements, designing cases, executing software and reporting results. Objectives can include finding defects, assessing quality, reducing risk, checking contractual or regulatory requirements and building justified confidence. Verification asks whether specified requirements are met; validation asks whether the product meets stakeholder needs in its use context. Debugging investigates and removes the cause of a failure. A tester can reveal a failure without repairing its cause.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A checkout test reveals that a coupon increases the total. The tester records inputs, observed results and expected results. A developer locates a sign error, changes the code and runs component checks. The tester then confirms the fix and checks related discount behavior. Finding the failure was testing; diagnosing and repairing it was debugging.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Testing is broader than executing code, and a successful test does not prove that every defect has been removed.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: A team reviews an unimplemented password requirement and finds ambiguity. Is this testing? Yes: static testing evaluates a work product without executing the software. Does the review debug code? No: no failure is being diagnosed and repaired.

lessons.title: 1.2 · Why testing matters
lessons.summary: Learn and practise why testing matters.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Testing can prevent defects through early review and detect defects before users experience failures. Its evidence supports release decisions and reduces the cost of later rework. Quality assurance is concerned with improving processes; testing is a product-oriented quality-control activity. An error is a human mistake. A defect is a flaw in a work product. A failure is observed incorrect behavior when a defect is triggered. A root cause is an underlying reason that helps explain why the mistake or defect arose.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A rushed developer misreads an unclear fee rule (error), writes the wrong comparison (defect), and customers are charged incorrectly for one account class (failure). An absent requirement review may be a root cause. Repairing the comparison addresses this defect; improving requirement reviews may prevent similar defects.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: A defect need not cause a failure on every execution. Testing and QA contribute to quality through different activities; testing does not guarantee quality by itself.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Would correcting the comparison alone eliminate the underlying process weakness? No. Would reviewing the fee requirement be useful before coding? Yes: it can expose ambiguity before it becomes an implementation defect.

lessons.title: 1.3 · Seven testing principles
lessons.summary: Learn and practise seven testing principles.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Remember seven ideas: tests can show defects but cannot establish their absence; exhaustive testing is generally infeasible; early testing saves resources; defects often cluster; tests lose effectiveness when repeatedly used without revision; testing depends on context; and a defect-free implementation can still fail to meet user needs. Use risk to choose where effort matters. Refresh tests when risks or behavior change, while retaining useful regression checks. Clustering is an observation that guides investigation, not a rule that untested areas are safe.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A mobile banking team discovers many failures in currency conversion and invests more testing there. It also checks critical login and transfer workflows. Repeating an unchanged currency suite for months stops finding new issues, so the team adds combinations suggested by recent changes and incidents.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Absence of observed failures is not proof of absence of defects. “Tests wear out” does not mean deleting the regression suite.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: A product satisfies every written requirement but customers cannot complete their main task. Which principle explains this? The absence-of-defects fallacy: meeting a specification does not establish usefulness.

lessons.title: 1.4 · Test activities, testware and roles
lessons.summary: Learn and practise test activities, testware and roles.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Planning defines objectives, approach, resources and criteria. Monitoring compares progress with the plan; control adjusts actions. Analysis identifies what to test from the test basis. Design decides how to test and develops cases and coverage items. Implementation prepares procedures, suites, data and environments. Execution runs tests and records outcomes. Completion consolidates evidence, archives useful testware and captures lessons. Activities overlap and depend on risk, lifecycle, constraints and stakeholders. Testware includes plans, conditions, cases, procedures, data, logs and reports. Traceability links the basis, conditions, tests, results and defects. A test-management role coordinates the work; a testing role performs technical activities. One person may perform both.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Requirement R7 links to condition C3, cases T8 and T9, execution E2 and defect D4. When R7 changes, these links identify affected tests. A test log records observations; a completion report summarizes outcomes and unresolved risk for a release decision.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Analysis identifies conditions; design derives cases; implementation prepares executable testware. A job title does not uniquely determine a testing role.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: A team prepares accounts and a reusable execution procedure. Which activity? Implementation. It then compares executed cases against the target and changes priorities. Which activities? Monitoring and control.

lessons.title: 1.5 · Skills, teamwork and independence
lessons.summary: Learn and practise skills, teamwork and independence.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Useful tester skills include analytical thinking, curiosity, care, communication, domain understanding and technical knowledge. Communicate observable facts without blaming people. In a whole-team approach, quality is a shared responsibility and people contribute complementary skills; testers help others develop testing competence. Independence can reveal assumptions that authors share, but excessive separation can weaken collaboration, create bottlenecks or shift perceived ownership of quality away from developers. Choose a degree of independence appropriate to the risk and context.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A tester discusses a confusing delivery rule with a business specialist and developer. The specialist clarifies user needs, the tester proposes examples, and the developer explains technical constraints. A separately assigned reviewer later challenges an assumption all three missed.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Independence is not a reason to isolate testers. A whole-team approach does not remove specialist skills or make everyone equally capable of every task.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Rewrite “Your code is broken” as useful feedback. Example: “For account type X on build 18, the displayed fee is 12; the agreed example expects 10. These steps reproduce it.”

lessons.title: 2.1 · Testing across development lifecycles
lessons.summary: Learn and practise testing across development lifecycles.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Sequential lifecycles often connect planned test levels to corresponding development activities. Iterative and incremental development needs testing of new increments and regression of existing behavior. Across lifecycles, involve testers early, associate testing with development work, review work products when available and plan test levels with appropriate objectives. TDD uses component tests before implementation; ATDD starts from agreed acceptance examples; BDD expresses expected behavior in business-readable scenarios. DevOps encourages collaboration, automation and rapid feedback, while requiring reliable environments and maintained pipelines. Shift left moves suitable testing earlier; it complements testing later in delivery. Retrospectives examine outcomes and agree improvements whose effects should be checked.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: During refinement, three roles agree an acceptance example. A developer writes a failing check, implements behavior and refactors after it passes. A delivery pipeline runs checks on commits and deploys to a controlled environment. A retrospective discovers flaky test data and assigns an owner to fix it.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Shift left does not eliminate system or acceptance testing. Automated pipelines are useful only when their feedback is trustworthy.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: An action item says “improve testing.” Make it actionable. Example: “By next iteration, stabilize the five flaky checkout cases and compare rerun frequency before and after.”

lessons.title: 2.2 · Test levels, types and change checks
lessons.summary: Learn and practise test levels, types and change checks.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Component testing checks individual components; component integration checks interactions among components; system testing checks the whole system; system integration checks interactions with other systems or services; acceptance testing assesses readiness and stakeholder needs. Test levels differ in objects, objectives, basis, responsibilities and typical defects. Functional testing examines what a system does; non-functional testing examines qualities such as performance or usability. Black-box testing uses behavior without relying on internal structure; white-box testing derives checks from structure. Confirmation testing checks whether a specific defect was fixed. Regression testing checks whether a change adversely affected existing behavior.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: After repairing tax rounding, rerunning the failing rounding case is confirmation. Checking discounts, invoices and refunds is regression. Measuring response time under load is non-functional testing. Checking exchange of messages with a payment gateway is system integration.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: A test level is not a test type. The same test type can be applied at multiple levels, and regression can follow changes outside source code.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: A user representative checks whether a payroll product supports the agreed month-end workflow. Which level is the primary focus? Acceptance. If an API contract with a bank is checked instead, system integration is the focus.

lessons.title: 2.3 · Maintenance testing
lessons.summary: Learn and practise maintenance testing.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Maintenance testing evaluates changes to operational software and the effects on existing behavior. Triggers include modifications, migrations and retirement. A defect fix, operating-system update, infrastructure migration or changed configuration can create risk even when application code is untouched. Impact analysis identifies affected components, interfaces, data and stakeholders, then helps select confirmation and regression scope. Scope depends on change size, system size and risk.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A business moves its reporting database to a new platform. Tests check migrated data, queries, permissions, integrations and critical existing reports. Before retiring the old service, the team checks archival access and retention obligations.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Maintenance testing is not restricted to bug fixes. A seemingly small platform change may affect many consumers.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: What should guide regression selection after a library upgrade? Impact analysis and risk, including dependencies and interfaces; the number of changed application lines is insufficient.

lessons.title: 3.1 · Static testing
lessons.summary: Learn and practise static testing.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Static testing examines work products without executing the software under test. Reviews can examine requirements, user stories, designs, source code, test cases, contracts and user documentation. Static analysis tools can inspect suitably structured artifacts for issues such as unreachable code, inconsistent interfaces or coding-rule violations. Early static testing finds defects directly and can prevent expensive later rework. Dynamic testing executes software and reveals failures. Both provide complementary evidence: static review can find missing or contradictory requirements, while dynamic testing can assess behavior and runtime qualities.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A requirement says “respond quickly.” A review exposes missing measurable acceptance criteria before code exists. Static analysis identifies an unused variable in source. A load test later measures whether the implemented service meets the agreed response-time target.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Static testing finds defects directly; dynamic testing observes failures that may lead to defect investigation. Static testing does not require executable code.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Can a test plan be statically tested? Yes: a review can reveal missing scope, inconsistent criteria or invalid assumptions. Can response time under actual load be established by that review? No: runtime evidence is needed.

lessons.title: 3.2 · Feedback and review process
lessons.summary: Learn and practise feedback and review process.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Early and frequent stakeholder feedback helps align understanding and discover changes before they become costly. A review typically involves planning, initiation, individual review, communication and analysis, then fixing and reporting. The author creates and updates the work product. Reviewers identify anomalies. A moderator facilitates effective meetings. A scribe records findings and decisions. A review leader coordinates the review; management supplies resources. Informal reviews have little prescribed process; walkthroughs are usually author-led; technical reviews involve qualified peers and aim at evaluation or consensus; inspections use the most formal process with defined roles and collected information. Clear objectives, suitable participants, small manageable work products, preparation and a constructive culture support success.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: For a payment specification, reviewers first inspect individually using a checklist. The moderator keeps the meeting focused on anomalies. The author clarifies findings, the scribe records decisions, and unresolved issues are tracked after the meeting.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Roles describe responsibilities, not necessarily separate people. A review should evaluate the work product rather than the author’s performance.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Which activity comes before discussing findings in a formal review? Individual review. Which role writes down agreed findings during the meeting? The scribe.

lessons.title: 4.1 · Choosing test techniques
lessons.summary: Learn and practise choosing test techniques.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Black-box techniques derive tests from specified behavior and do not require knowledge of implementation. White-box techniques derive tests from internal structure. Experience-based techniques draw on knowledge of past failures, domain risks and tester judgment. Techniques identify coverage items and help create a defensible selection of cases. They can be combined: requirements tell you what users need, structure reveals unexercised paths, and experience suggests likely problems.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A fee rule is tested with partitions of customer types (black-box). The team checks unexecuted decision outcomes (white-box). A tester adds a locale case after recalling a previous decimal-separator defect (experience-based).

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Black-box does not mean informal. Knowing the source code does not prevent you from deriving a test from a requirement.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: A case is selected because a decision outcome has never run. What is the basis? Structure, so this is white-box. A case selected because a business rule distinguishes two account classes is black-box.

lessons.title: 4.2 · Black-box techniques in practice
lessons.summary: Learn and practise black-box techniques in practice.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Equivalence partitioning divides a data domain into groups expected to be processed similarly; test each relevant valid and invalid partition. Boundary value analysis focuses on edges of ordered partitions. Two-value BVA uses each boundary and its closest value in the adjacent partition; three-value BVA adds the closest neighbor inside the partition. Decision tables relate condition combinations to actions: list conditions, enumerate feasible combinations, specify actions and derive cases for rules. Merge rules only when differences cannot affect actions. State transition testing models states, events and resulting states. State coverage, valid-transition coverage and all-transition coverage measure different items; tests for invalid transitions check rejected behavior without masking defects by chaining invalid events.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: An integer quantity is accepted from 3 to 7. EP partitions are below 3, 3–7 and above 7; representatives 2, 5 and 8 cover them. Two-value BVA uses 2,3,7,8; three-value BVA uses 2,3,4,6,7,8. Two independent Boolean conditions yield four combinations before excluding infeasible rules. A door model has Closed → Open on unlock and Open → Closed on lock; visiting both states need not exercise every event.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Partition coverage is not coverage of every combination of partitions. Boundaries apply to ordered partitions. Reaching every state does not guarantee traversing every transition.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: For 1–5 inclusive integers, give three-value BVA inputs. Solution: 0,1,2,4,5,6. For a rule requiring both consent and an active account, which combination permits access? Both true; the other three combinations deny access.

lessons.title: 4.3 · White-box coverage
lessons.summary: Learn and practise white-box coverage.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Statement coverage is executed executable statements divided by total executable statements. Branch coverage is executed control-flow branches divided by total branches. Use the model given in the question to identify branches; conditional decisions generally have both true and false outcomes. Full branch coverage implies full statement coverage for the modeled executable structure, but full statement coverage can miss a branch. Structural coverage can expose untested implementation and support useful checks, but it cannot reveal behavior that was never implemented merely by reaching code.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Pseudocode: if member then applyDiscount; printTotal. A member test executes both statements, achieving full statement coverage, but misses the false outcome of the decision. Adding a non-member test exercises that branch. If four of five executable statements run, statement coverage is 4/5 × 100 = 80%.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Do not infer branch coverage from a statement percentage. Even 100% coverage does not establish correctness or complete requirements coverage.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: A model has eight branches; six run. Coverage is 6/8 × 100 = 75%. What additional evidence is needed before calling the product correct? Assertions against expected behavior, requirements and risk-based tests beyond structural reachability.

lessons.title: 4.4 · Experience-based techniques
lessons.summary: Learn and practise experience-based techniques.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Error guessing uses knowledge of typical mistakes and previous defects to propose tests. Exploratory testing combines learning, design and execution as the tester responds to observations; it is often organized into time-boxed sessions with charters, notes and debriefs. Checklist-based testing uses a maintained list of conditions to guide consistent checking while allowing judgment in the detailed cases. All three can complement systematic techniques, particularly where specifications are incomplete. Their effectiveness depends on relevant expertise and on documenting enough evidence to communicate results.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A tester guesses that a copied discount rule might mishandle a zero amount. In an exploratory session with a “recover after payment interruption” charter, observations guide the next checks. A release checklist reminds the team to verify keyboard access, validation messages and recovery from network loss.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Exploratory testing is not unrecorded random clicking. A checklist guides coverage but is not automatically a detailed executable procedure.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Which technique best fits a 45-minute investigation where each result informs the next experiment? Exploratory testing. How can the session remain accountable? Use a charter, record observations and summarize coverage and findings.

lessons.title: 4.5 · Collaborative acceptance testing
lessons.summary: Learn and practise collaborative acceptance testing.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: User stories describe a user, a need and its value. The card is a starting point for conversation; confirmation is captured in acceptance criteria. Business representatives, developers and testers develop a shared understanding through examples. Acceptance criteria may be scenario-oriented, such as Given/When/Then, or rule-oriented, such as a checklist of constraints. Criteria define what must be met and should support unambiguous evaluation. ATDD derives acceptance tests collaboratively before implementation; include positive, negative and relevant non-functional cases and resolve inconsistent examples early.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Story: “As a subscriber, I want to pause renewals so I can avoid unwanted charges.” Criterion: Given an active subscription, when the user pauses before the renewal cutoff, then no renewal charge is made. Tests should cover a timely pause, a request after cutoff, an already paused account and resumption according to agreed rules.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: A story is not complete simply because its card exists. Acceptance criteria describe behavior; they need not prescribe implementation details.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Criterion: purchases of at least 50 qualify for free delivery. An ATDD case uses a total of 50 and expects zero delivery charge; a negative case uses 49.99 and expects the specified paid-delivery amount. Agree that amount before automating the case.

lessons.title: 5.1 · Planning, estimates and priorities
lessons.summary: Learn and practise planning, estimates and priorities.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: A test plan states objectives, scope, approach, resources, schedule, responsibilities and criteria. Testers contribute to release and iteration planning by identifying risks, testability concerns and effort. Entry criteria describe conditions for starting an activity; exit criteria describe conditions for completion. Estimate effort from relevant historical ratios, extrapolation, expert consensus or three-point estimates. In the three-point formula used here, E = (optimistic + 4 × most likely + pessimistic) / 6. State assumptions and uncertainty. Prioritize by risk, coverage or requirements importance, then account for dependencies and resources. A test pyramid favors many small fast checks and fewer broad slower checks. Testing quadrants organize technology/business focus and support/critiquing purpose: Q1 component checks, Q2 business-facing examples supporting work, Q3 business-facing evaluation, Q4 technology-facing quality evaluation. A related three-point uncertainty estimate is SD=(pessimistic−optimistic)/6; for O=6 and P=18 days, SD=2 days. This is distinct from expected effort.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: For O=4, M=7 and P=16 hours, E=(4+28+16)/6=8 hours. If execution of a high-risk payment test requires account setup, setup must run first. A coverage-based order starts with the case covering the most items; additional-coverage ordering then chooses cases covering the most still-uncovered items.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: An estimate is not a commitment without uncertainty. Highest priority does not override a prerequisite. Quadrants are not chronological phases or fixed test levels.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Three teams report 10, 14 and 18 hours. Can their arithmetic mean alone remove uncertainty? No: discuss assumptions. If T1 covers A,B,C; T2 covers B,C; T3 covers D,E, additional-coverage order is T1,T3,T2.

lessons.title: 5.2 · Risk management
lessons.summary: Learn and practise risk management.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: A risk is an uncertain event with possible adverse consequences. Risk level combines likelihood and impact, often by multiplication of agreed scales. Project risks threaten delivery, such as staff loss or unavailable environments. Product risks threaten product quality, such as wrong payments or insecure access. Product risk analysis identifies and assesses risks; it guides scope, effort, techniques, coverage and priority. Possible responses include mitigation, acceptance, transfer and contingency planning. Testing reduces uncertainty and can reduce the probability of delivering defects, but residual risk remains and must be communicated.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Risk A has likelihood 2 and impact 5, level 10; risk B has likelihood 4 and impact 2, level 8. Under that model A ranks higher. Delayed environment delivery is a project risk; incorrect transaction totals are a product risk. More thorough checks may be allocated to totals because financial consequences are severe.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: Risk likelihood is not impact. Multiplying ordinal ratings is a prioritization convention, not a precise probability of loss. A passing suite does not erase residual risk.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: A release contains an untested authentication change. What should a status report include? The affected risk, missing evidence, consequences and proposed actions so the decision-maker can make an informed acceptance or mitigation decision.

lessons.title: 5.3 · Monitoring, control and communication
lessons.summary: Learn and practise monitoring, control and communication.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Monitor progress, coverage, defects, effort, cost and quality signals against the plan. Metrics need context: counts of executed tests say little without scope, results and risk. Control actions may change priorities, resources, schedule or scope in response to evidence. Progress reports support ongoing decisions; completion reports summarize achieved objectives, results, deviations and unresolved risks at a milestone. Tailor detail and format to the audience. Developers may need reproducible findings; managers need consequences and decisions; distributed teams benefit from clear written records in addition to discussion.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A report says 80 of 100 tests ran, with 12 failures concentrated in checkout and 20 security cases blocked by an environment issue. A manager sees release exposure, while engineers receive failure details. A control action restores the environment and brings high-risk security checks forward.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: A high pass percentage can conceal missing high-risk coverage. Reports should distinguish what was tested from what remains unknown.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: The plan expects 90 executions, but 45 are complete. Identifying the deviation is monitoring; deciding to reallocate engineers is control. For a release meeting, include residual risk and decision requests rather than only raw logs.

lessons.title: 5.4 · Configuration management
lessons.summary: Learn and practise configuration management.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Configuration management identifies, versions, controls and relates items needed for reproducible testing. Relevant items include requirements, builds, tests, data, environment configuration and results. A baseline is an agreed set of versions that can be referenced consistently. Traceability plus version control helps determine which result applies to which product and test basis. Controlled changes make impact analysis and investigation more reliable.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A test result links application build 82, requirement revision 4, test suite 11 and data set 6. When a failure cannot be reproduced on build 83, the team can restore the original baseline and compare the change.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: A test result detached from its build and environment may be misleading even if the test passed. Versioning source code alone does not control all test dependencies.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Which information makes a data-dependent failure reproducible? The product version, procedure, environment and data version, as well as actual and expected results. “It failed last week” is insufficient.

lessons.title: 5.5 · Writing actionable defect reports
lessons.summary: Learn and practise writing actionable defect reports.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: A defect report should let its audience understand impact, reproduce the observation and assess next actions. Include a clear title, unique reference, reporter and date, affected product and environment, preconditions, reproducible steps, actual and expected results, supporting evidence, severity, priority and status as appropriate. Severity describes impact; priority describes urgency. Keep observations distinct from hypotheses about the cause. A reported anomaly may require investigation before it is confirmed as a defect.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Title: “Expired coupon increases order total on build 82.” Preconditions: basket total 40 and coupon expired yesterday. Steps: open checkout, enter coupon, apply. Expected: coupon rejected and total remains 40. Actual: total becomes 45. Attach the request ID and screenshot; record browser and build. This gives an investigator an actionable starting point.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: A dramatic title or guessed implementation fix does not replace reproduction steps. Severity and priority may differ; a small visible issue can be urgent for a launch.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: A report says “Login is bad” and includes no account state. Improve it by naming the build, account conditions, exact actions, observed message and expected result. Describe what happened before asserting a root cause.

lessons.title: 6.1 · Tool support
lessons.summary: Learn and practise tool support.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Tools can support management, static analysis, design and implementation, execution, comparison of results, performance measurement, coverage, collaboration and delivery pipelines. Select tools for the activity and the information needed. Test-management tools organize cases, execution and reporting. Static analysis examines work products without running the software. Execution tools run checks and compare observations with expectations. Performance tools generate load and gather timing and resource evidence. Tools improve efficiency only when processes, skills and integration support their use.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: An execution harness runs service checks; a coverage tool reports unvisited branches; a performance tool creates concurrent traffic; a management tool connects cases and results to requirements. These tools answer different questions and can exchange data.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: A tool does not remove the need to choose useful tests or interpret results. Recording a workflow alone does not produce a robust oracle.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: Which tool fits identifying unreachable code before execution? Static analysis. Which fits organizing release coverage and linking failures to cases? Test management.

lessons.title: 6.2 · Automation benefits and risks
lessons.summary: Learn and practise automation benefits and risks.

blocks.title: Understand
blocks.text: Automation can make repeated checks faster and more consistent, reduce manual repetition, enable unattended execution and provide rapid feedback. Costs include implementation, maintenance, training and infrastructure. Risks include unrealistic expectations, poorly chosen checks, fragile dependencies, incorrect oracles, flaky results and overreliance on tool output. Use a pilot to learn integration costs and evaluate value. Preserve human investigation, exploratory work and judgment where they add evidence. Automated passing checks mean that the implemented checks passed under their conditions.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: A stable API regression suite gives feedback on each commit. A recorded interface script fails after harmless layout changes and takes hours to maintain. The team moves checks to an appropriate layer and retains a smaller set of user workflow checks.

blocks.title: Common exam trap
blocks.text: More automated tests does not automatically mean better coverage. Maintenance effort and signal reliability belong in the business case.

blocks.title: Self-check and solution
blocks.text: A tool produces many false alarms. Is faster execution enough to justify it? No: consider investigation and maintenance costs. A useful pilot measures reliable feedback and value, not just the number of scripts generated.

lessons.title: Final revision · Turn evidence into a study decision
lessons.summary: Review distinctions, calculations and timed-exam strategy.

blocks.title: Recall and distinguish
blocks.text: Explain testing versus debugging; error versus defect versus failure; analysis versus design versus implementation; test level versus test type; confirmation versus regression; static versus dynamic; statement versus branch coverage; entry versus exit criteria; severity versus priority; project versus product risk. Give a concrete example for each distinction rather than memorizing a label.

blocks.title: Technique checklist
blocks.text: For EP, list valid and invalid partitions before choosing representatives. For BVA, state whether two or three values are required and the input resolution. For decision tables, enumerate feasible rules before merging. For state models, count states and transitions separately. For estimation, show the formula and units. For prioritization, check dependencies and additional coverage. For defect reports, specify reproducible actions and observable expected results.

blocks.title: Timed strategy
blocks.text: Read selection counts carefully. Make one pass through straightforward items and leave time for longer application questions. Use the exact information and technique named in the question. Unanswered items score zero. Answers and explanations become available after submitting the mock or when its timer expires.

blocks.title: Review after a paper
blocks.text: For each mistake, identify the objective, explain why the chosen option failed, solve the relevant lesson example again and write a new example. Treat guesses as review targets even when correct. Use objective practice for weak areas. A repeated paper is useful revision but cannot supply fresh readiness evidence. Confirm registration and exam arrangements with your provider.

questions.prompt: Which activity is a typical objective of testing?

options.text: Assigning development salaries
Negotiating office rental terms
Selecting the product's sales channel
Providing evidence for a release decision

questions.explanation: Testing supplies information about quality and risk for stakeholder decisions. Salaries, sales channels and rental agreements are organizational activities rather than typical test objectives. Syllabus reference: FL-1.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: What does the whole-team approach make a shared responsibility?

options.text: Formal inspection moderation
Product quality
Signing supplier contracts
Performance-tool administration

questions.explanation: The team shares responsibility for quality and brings complementary skills. Specific specialist duties and commercial sign-off do not become collective obligations merely because the team uses this approach. Syllabus reference: FL-1.5.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: A developer investigates a failing calculation, identifies a wrong operator and repairs it. Which activity is being described?

options.text: Test monitoring
Debugging
Acceptance testing
Test analysis

questions.explanation: Debugging locates and removes a failure's cause. Analysis identifies conditions to test, monitoring compares progress with plans, and acceptance testing evaluates readiness for stakeholder use. Syllabus reference: FL-1.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A reporting product passes every written requirement but users cannot produce the report needed for their daily work. Which principle best explains the problem?

options.text: Tests wear out
Absence-of-defects fallacy
Defect clustering
Early testing saves resources

questions.explanation: Meeting specified requirements does not ensure that a product meets user needs. The stem concerns usefulness, rather than clustered defects, repeated tests or when testing begins. Syllabus reference: FL-1.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester studies a billing specification and identifies conditions that need checking. Which activity is the main focus?

options.text: Test implementation
Test completion
Test execution
Test analysis

questions.explanation: Analysis determines what to test from the basis. Implementation prepares procedures and environments, execution runs checks, and completion consolidates and archives outcomes. Syllabus reference: FL-1.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A safety-critical device and a disposable game prototype use different test approaches. What best explains this choice?

options.text: Risk, regulation and constraints shape the method
Their teams must use identical exit criteria
Their source-code languages define all testing needs
Their release dates determine the correctness of results

questions.explanation: Testing depends on context, including risk, regulation, stakeholders and resources. A language or date alone cannot determine the entire approach, and identical criteria need not suit both products. Syllabus reference: FL-1.4.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which testware is most directly created when preparing an ordered procedure for running several test cases?

options.text: A defect status summary
A test completion report
A product risk register
A test script

questions.explanation: An execution procedure or script is implementation testware. Risks support planning; completion reports summarize finished work; defect status summaries concern findings rather than executable steps. Syllabus reference: FL-1.4.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester needs to discuss a reproducible failure with its author. Which response best demonstrates constructive communication?

options.text: Delay the report until a different tester can present it
Rank the author's competence in the defect title
State a root cause before investigating the failure
Give observable outcomes and concrete steps to repeat the issue

questions.explanation: Specific observations and reproduction steps support investigation without blame. Personal criticism, unsupported diagnosis and unnecessary delay undermine useful communication. Syllabus reference: FL-1.5.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which testing practice is useful across development lifecycles?

options.text: Replace component checks with stakeholder acceptance
Wait for implementation to end before designing checks
Give component and system testing identical objectives
Review suitable draft requirements and designs early

questions.explanation: Early review can prevent downstream defects across lifecycles. Delaying all testing, replacing lower-level checks or using identical objectives at every level removes useful evidence. Syllabus reference: FL-2.1.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which approach begins with component tests before writing the corresponding implementation?

options.text: Test-driven development
Risk-based testing
Checklist-based testing
Exploratory testing

questions.explanation: TDD uses a failing component test to guide implementation and refactoring. Exploratory testing integrates learning and execution; risk-based testing prioritizes by risk; checklists guide conditions to inspect. Syllabus reference: FL-2.1.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: A team checks interactions between a tax-calculation component and a pricing component within one application. Which level is the primary focus?

options.text: System integration testing
Acceptance testing
Component integration testing
Component testing

questions.explanation: Component integration targets interactions among components. Component testing isolates a component; system integration concerns interactions among systems; acceptance assesses stakeholder readiness. Syllabus reference: FL-2.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A fix corrects the original tax-rounding failure. Why also run previously passing discount tests?

options.text: To diagnose the operator that caused the original defect
To detect unintended effects of the change
To replace confirmation testing of the repaired behavior
To establish that no defects remain in the application

questions.explanation: Regression testing checks for adverse effects on existing behavior. Diagnosis belongs to debugging; a passing suite cannot prove absence of defects, and confirmation of the fix remains useful. Syllabus reference: FL-2.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: An application is delivered in small increments. Which test planning response is appropriate?

options.text: Reuse the first increment's cases without reviewing changes
Limit every iteration to acceptance testing of new features
Postpone design of test cases until the final increment
Test each increment and consider regression of existing behavior

questions.explanation: Incremental development needs checks of new behavior and potentially affected existing behavior. Waiting until the end or ignoring changes loses timely feedback; one level cannot address every risk. Syllabus reference: FL-2.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A DevOps pipeline gives rapid automated feedback, but intermittently reports failures caused by unstable test data. What should the team address?

options.text: The removal of all manual investigation
The use of slower deployments as the sole quality measure
Stabilize the data and improve signal reliability
The replacement of every review with pipeline execution

questions.explanation: Unreliable feedback consumes investigation effort and reduces trust. DevOps still needs human judgment and reviews; deployment speed alone does not establish quality. Syllabus reference: FL-2.1.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which work product can be assessed through static testing before any executable application exists?

options.text: An execution of the application's binary
A live session exercising implemented checkout behavior
A draft user story
A measured production response-time trace generated by the new application

questions.explanation: A user story can be reviewed without executing the software. The other choices depend on execution or implemented behavior and describe runtime evidence or activity. Syllabus reference: FL-3.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: What is a benefit of early stakeholder feedback on a draft workflow?

options.text: Discovering mismatched expectations before implementation
Replacing the need for an agreed test basis
Eliminating the need to assess implemented behavior
Guaranteeing that stakeholders will never change priorities

questions.explanation: Feedback can expose misunderstanding while changes are cheaper. It neither prevents future changes nor removes dynamic testing or the need for shared expectations. Syllabus reference: FL-3.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: A review finds contradictory fee rules before coding starts. Why does this add value?

options.text: It can prevent implementing inconsistent behavior
It proves that the future implementation has no defects
It demonstrates runtime performance under peak load
It replaces the need to test fee calculations after coding

questions.explanation: Early defect detection can avoid rework and failures downstream. A requirements review does not measure runtime performance, certify future code or replace complementary dynamic checks. Syllabus reference: FL-3.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Reviewers have individually recorded anomalies in a design. What is the next main review activity?

options.text: Communicate and analyze the findings
Archive the final test execution logs
Skip to closure without evaluating anomalies
Deploy the implementation to production

questions.explanation: After individual review, participants discuss and analyze anomalies before fixing and reporting. Deployment and execution logs are unrelated steps; unresolved findings should not simply be ignored. Syllabus reference: FL-3.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO examples of black-box test derivation.

options.text: Choose a case because a similar product once failed there
Choose cases from combinations of business-rule conditions
Choose a case to execute an unvisited source-code branch
Choose inputs from specified valid and invalid age ranges

questions.explanation: Partitions and decision tables derive from specified behavior. An unvisited branch uses internal structure, while prior failure experience motivates error guessing. Syllabus reference: FL-4.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: An input executes all executable statements in a function. What follows about statement coverage?

options.text: Requirements-based acceptance coverage is complete
It is 100% for that function
The business specification contains no ambiguity
That function’s false decision outcome has also run

questions.explanation: Executing all statements establishes full statement coverage. It says nothing conclusive about branch outcomes, missing requirements or correctness, so those stronger claims are unsupported. Syllabus reference: FL-4.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A decision has true and false outcomes. Existing tests exercise only the true outcome. What improves its branch coverage?

options.text: Repeat the true-outcome test with a new test name
Increase the number of assertions on the true path
Inspect the same execution log a second time
Add an input that takes the unvisited path

questions.explanation: The missing branch is the false outcome; executing it improves coverage. Renaming, rereading or adding assertions on an already exercised path does not execute a new branch. Syllabus reference: FL-4.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester adds cases for empty input after recalling earlier validation defects. Which technique is being used?

options.text: State transition testing
Statement testing
Error guessing
Decision table testing

questions.explanation: The choice is driven by experience with likely errors. No structural coverage, condition table or state model is used to derive the case in this scenario. Syllabus reference: FL-4.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: During a chartered session, each observation guides the tester's next experiment. Which technique best fits?

options.text: A formal inspection meeting
Exploratory testing
Three-point estimation
A fixed scripted regression run

questions.explanation: Exploratory testing combines learning, design and execution adaptively. Fixed scripts predefine the sequence; inspections review work products; estimation predicts effort rather than explores behavior. Syllabus reference: FL-4.4.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Business, development and testing discuss concrete examples for a user story. What is the main benefit?

options.text: A replacement for evaluation of completed functionality
A prescribed internal implementation for the agreed examples
A shared understanding of desired behavior
An implementation design sufficient to bypass reviews

questions.explanation: Collaboration clarifies needs and exposes differing assumptions. It need not dictate implementation and cannot guarantee defect-free requirements or remove later evaluation. Syllabus reference: FL-4.5.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A field accepts integer ages 18–65 inclusive. Values below 18 and above 65 are rejected for different reasons. Which set covers every stated equivalence partition?
questions.explanation: The three partitions are below 18, valid 18–65 and above 65. The correct set represents each. The other sets omit one or both invalid partitions; boundary coverage is not the requested measure. Syllabus reference: FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: An integer quantity is accepted from 3 through 7. Which set supplies two-value boundary analysis for both edges?
questions.explanation: Two-value BVA checks each boundary and its immediate adjacent-partition neighbor: 2/3 and 7/8. Interior neighbors belong to three-value coverage; distant values skip the nearest neighbors. Syllabus reference: FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: A discount is granted when an account is active AND a coupon is valid. Both conditions can independently be true or false. How many feasible rules are needed in the full, unminimized decision table?
questions.explanation: Two independent Boolean conditions give 2 × 2 = 4 combinations. One permits a discount and three deny it. Counting actions alone gives two, while eight would require a third independent Boolean condition. Syllabus reference: FL-4.2.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: Model: Locked --coin→ Unlocked; Unlocked --push→ Locked; Locked --push→ Locked; Unlocked --coin→ Unlocked. Starting Locked, events coin,push have run. What is valid-transition coverage?
questions.explanation: Two of the four specified valid transitions ran: Locked→Unlocked on coin and Unlocked→Locked on push. Both states were visited, but the two self-transitions were not, so state coverage must not be substituted. Syllabus reference: FL-4.2.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: Criterion: orders totaling at least 50 receive free delivery; lower totals cost 5. Which TWO acceptance examples test the threshold correctly?

options.text: Total 50 expects delivery charge 0
Total 49.99 expects delivery charge 0
Total 50 expects delivery charge 5
Total 49.99 expects delivery charge 5

questions.explanation: The rule includes 50 in the free-delivery class. The neighboring lower total stays in the paid class. The distractors reverse the expected results and would encode the wrong business rule. Syllabus reference: FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: How can a tester contribute during iteration planning?

options.text: Replace the product owner in ranking business value
Identify testability concerns and testing effort
Approve supplier invoices for the release
Set the organization's annual salary bands

questions.explanation: Testers contribute testing expertise, feasibility and effort information to planning. Commercial administration and business prioritization ownership are different responsibilities. Syllabus reference: FL-5.1.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: A team needs a document defining test scope, approach, resources and completion criteria. Which testware serves that purpose?

options.text: A test execution log
An automated test result
An individual defect report
A test plan

questions.explanation: A plan describes intended testing and its organization. Logs and results capture executed work; defect reports describe anomalies rather than the overall approach and resource commitments. Syllabus reference: FL-5.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which activity best fits the business-facing quadrant that critiques the product (Q3)?

options.text: Load testing of service throughput
Acceptance examples guiding implementation
Exploratory usability evaluation with users
Automated component checks of an internal function

questions.explanation: Q3 evaluates the product from a business or user perspective. Component checks fit Q1, technical performance evaluation fits Q4, and implementation-guiding acceptance examples fit Q2. Syllabus reference: FL-5.1.7 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which is a product risk rather than a project risk?

options.text: The released application calculates interest incorrectly
The test environment arrives two weeks late
A key tester becomes unavailable during the schedule
The supplier misses a planned handover date

questions.explanation: Incorrect interest is a potential product-quality problem. Staffing, environment delivery and supplier delays threaten execution of the project and its schedule. Syllabus reference: FL-5.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A release manager needs to decide whether to ship. Which report content is most useful?

options.text: The number of team meetings without testing outcomes
Achieved coverage, unresolved defects and residual risks
The names of test tools without their results
Every raw request log without an interpretation

questions.explanation: Decision-makers need evidence and its implications, including gaps and risk. Raw logs, meeting counts and tool names alone do not communicate readiness to release. Syllabus reference: FL-5.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why link an execution result to build, test-suite and data-set versions?

options.text: To avoid recording actual and expected results
To remove the need for impact analysis on changes
To make the evidence reproducible and attributable
To establish that later builds have identical behavior

questions.explanation: Configuration references identify what was tested and help reproduce findings. They do not replace result details, imply unchanged later builds or remove analysis of changes. Syllabus reference: FL-5.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Use E=(O+4M+P)/6. An effort estimate has O=4, M=7 and P=16 hours. What is E?

options.text: 7 hours
8 hours
9 hours
12 hours

questions.explanation: Substitution gives (4+28+16)/6=48/6=8 hours. Seven uses only the most-likely value; nine is the unweighted mean; twelve does not follow the specified formula. Syllabus reference: FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: For additional-coverage prioritization, T1 covers A,B,C; T2 covers B,C; T3 covers D,E. No dependencies apply. Which order is correct?
questions.explanation: T1 first adds three items. T3 next adds two still-uncovered items, while T2 adds none. Static total-coverage ordering would incorrectly place T2 second for the requested additional-coverage technique. Syllabus reference: FL-5.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: A report for a checkout failure already includes build, browser, account state and steps. Which addition most directly makes the anomaly evaluable?

options.text: Actual and expected totals linked to the pricing rule
A proposed database rewrite without observed outcomes
A list of unrelated defects from another product
A personal assessment of the developer's skill

questions.explanation: Specific actual and expected results tied to the basis let an investigator evaluate the anomaly. Proposed fixes, personal criticism and unrelated findings do not establish what failed. Syllabus reference: FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team needs to simulate concurrent users and measure response time. Which tool category is appropriate?

options.text: Performance testing tools
Configuration management tools
Test data cataloging tools
Static analysis tools

questions.explanation: Performance tools generate load and collect timing or resource evidence. Configuration tools version items, static analysis inspects work products, and catalogs organize data rather than measure behavior under load. Syllabus reference: FL-6.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO potential benefits of suitable test automation.

options.text: Proof that no defects remain
Rapid feedback after code changes
Elimination of test maintenance
Repeatable execution of routine checks

questions.explanation: Automation can execute repeatable checks and provide quick feedback. Scripts and infrastructure still need maintenance, and their passing results do not prove absence of defects. Syllabus reference: FL-6.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: How is testing commonly classified in relation to quality management?

options.text: A process-oriented quality-assurance audit
A product-oriented quality-control activity
A commercial product-positioning activity
A personnel performance-appraisal activity

questions.explanation: Testing evaluates work products and their quality, making it quality control. QA focuses on processes; commercial positioning and employee appraisal are not its classification. Syllabus reference: FL-1.2.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: What is an advantage of testers, developers and business representatives working as one team?

options.text: Assigning quality ownership exclusively to the testers
Combining complementary skills to solve quality problems
Making each person equally proficient in every tool
Removing the need for any specialized test knowledge

questions.explanation: Complementary skills improve problem solving and shared understanding. Whole-team working neither gives everyone identical expertise nor removes specialization; quality remains shared. Syllabus reference: FL-1.5.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: A hospital system is tested before a medication workflow is released. Which reason most directly justifies the effort?

options.text: Replace the need for review of medication requirements
Transfer responsibility for medical decisions to testers
Establish that every possible input has been exercised
Reduce the chance of harmful failures reaching users

questions.explanation: Testing provides evidence and reduces delivery risk, which matters where failures may harm users. Exhaustive testing is generally infeasible, and testing does not assume clinical responsibility or replace reviews. Syllabus reference: FL-1.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team reviews draft requirements before coding and resolves unclear rules. Which principle does this illustrate?

options.text: Tests wear out
Defects cluster together
Early testing saves time and money
Testing shows the absence of defects

questions.explanation: Resolving problems early avoids downstream implementation and rework. The situation does not involve repeated tests or clustering, and testing cannot establish absence of defects. Syllabus reference: FL-1.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which pair correctly links an activity to its typical testware?

options.text: Completion — new input partitions as its main output
Analysis — production deployment binaries
Planning — measured results from tests not yet executed
Execution — logs of observed outcomes

questions.explanation: Execution creates records of observations. Conditions and partitions concern analysis/design; binaries are implementation products of development; planning cannot record outcomes of future execution. Syllabus reference: FL-1.4.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A requirement changes, and links from it to cases identify which checks need revision. What benefit is being used?

options.text: Proof that all unlinked requirements are covered
Removal of the need to review the revised requirement
Impact assessment through traceability
Automatic repair of defects in the implementation

questions.explanation: Traceability enables impact analysis by relating basis and testware. Links do not perform reviews or code repairs, and absent links cannot prove coverage. Syllabus reference: FL-1.4.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: A small team member schedules testing and also derives cases. How should the roles be understood?

options.text: An individual can carry both responsibilities
Case derivation makes all scheduling a development role
The person must choose one role and abandon the other
Roles require different people even in a small team

questions.explanation: Roles describe responsibilities and can be combined. Scheduling is test management and derivation is technical testing; neither changes category because the same person performs it. Syllabus reference: FL-1.4.5 (K2).

questions.prompt: An independent tester challenges assumptions shared by the authors. What benefit does this illustrate?

options.text: Independent testers own all product quality
Independent testing makes communication unnecessary
A different perspective can reveal overlooked problems
Author-created checks lose all value once independence is added

questions.explanation: Independence can expose shared assumptions. Collaboration and shared quality responsibility still matter, and developer checks continue to provide useful evidence. Syllabus reference: FL-1.5.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which statement describes good coordination of development and testing?

options.text: Every development activity requires only production monitoring
Testers should avoid draft work products until sign-off
Testing activities should share one identical objective
Each test level has objectives suited to that level

questions.explanation: Different levels address different objects and goals. One objective for all levels loses their distinctions; production monitoring alone omits earlier evidence, and suitable drafts can be reviewed. Syllabus reference: FL-2.1.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which approach expresses expected behavior as business-readable scenarios before implementing it?

options.text: Behavior-driven development
Defect density analysis
Configuration baselining
Behavior-based coverage measurement

questions.explanation: BDD uses behavior-focused examples, often in Given/When/Then form, to guide shared understanding and development. Coverage, defect metrics and baselines serve different purposes. Syllabus reference: FL-2.1.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: A service is checked for response time and resource usage under peak traffic. Which type of testing is the main focus?

options.text: Non-functional testing
Confirmation testing
Functional rule testing
Static requirements review

questions.explanation: Timing and resource characteristics are non-functional qualities. Confirmation concerns a specific fix; functional testing checks what the system does; static review cannot measure live load behavior. Syllabus reference: FL-2.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: The application code is unchanged, but its database platform is upgraded. What testing response is appropriate?

options.text: Treat the upgrade as outside all testing responsibilities
Assume a previously passing result applies to the new platform
Run only the first component test ever written
Assess affected behavior and perform maintenance testing

questions.explanation: Platform changes can affect queries, data and integrations even without source changes. Impact analysis guides maintenance scope; arbitrary tests or old evidence do not establish compatibility. Syllabus reference: FL-2.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A retrospective agrees an improvement but assigns no owner or follow-up. What should be added?

options.text: An actionable experiment with ownership and outcome review
A guarantee that the same issue cannot recur
A restriction to measuring individual performance
A replacement of all technical discussion with voting

questions.explanation: Retrospectives should produce useful improvements and assess their effects. Guarantees, eliminating discussion or blaming individuals do not make actions effective. Syllabus reference: FL-2.1.6 (K2).

questions.prompt: Reviewing acceptance examples during refinement instead of waiting for completed code is an example of what?

options.text: Delaying feedback until the release decision
Moving suitable testing earlier
Replacing system testing with code review
Moving all checks into production

questions.explanation: Shift left moves suitable activities earlier, including review of examples. It complements rather than replaces later testing and does not mean shifting work into production or postponing feedback. Syllabus reference: FL-2.1.5 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which review role primarily facilitates an effective review meeting?

options.text: Manager
Scribe
Author
Moderator

questions.explanation: The moderator facilitates communication and keeps the meeting useful. The author creates the artifact, the scribe records findings and management provides resources and support. Syllabus reference: FL-3.2.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which factor contributes to a successful review?

options.text: The artifact is as large as possible for every session
Findings are discouraged to protect the schedule
Participants prepare against clear objectives
The meeting evaluates the author's personal worth

questions.explanation: Preparation and clear aims support meaningful evaluation. Personal appraisal, oversized artifacts and suppressing findings undermine effectiveness and constructive feedback. Syllabus reference: FL-3.2.5 (K1).

questions.prompt: Select TWO accurate distinctions between static and dynamic testing.

options.text: Static review can find ambiguity in an unimplemented requirement
Dynamic testing identifies defects directly without observing execution
Dynamic testing executes software to observe behavior
Static testing measures live throughput by running the application

questions.explanation: Static testing examines artifacts without execution and can reveal ambiguity. Dynamic testing observes behavior through execution; live throughput is dynamic and failure observations may need further diagnosis. Syllabus reference: FL-3.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A review is author-led and takes participants through a work product to build understanding and gather findings. Which review type best fits?

options.text: Walkthrough
Inspection
Performance benchmark
Static analysis scan

questions.explanation: Walkthroughs are typically led by the author and can educate participants or find anomalies. Inspections are more formally organized; scans and benchmarks are tool or execution activities rather than this review type. Syllabus reference: FL-3.2.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester derives cases from source-code control flow. What makes these white-box cases?

options.text: They are written by the original developer
They are necessarily automated
Their coverage items come from internal structure
They require a user representative to choose inputs

questions.explanation: The basis for derivation defines the technique family. Automation, author identity and stakeholder participation do not by themselves make a case white-box. Syllabus reference: FL-4.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A function runs both outcomes of each modeled conditional decision. What evidence is established?

options.text: Consistent behavior in future configurations
Full branch coverage
Completion of requirements-based acceptance
Execution of each input-data combination

questions.explanation: Executing both outcomes covers the corresponding branches. It does not exhaust input combinations, detect omitted functionality or guarantee behavior in other environments. Syllabus reference: FL-4.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: An implementation omits a required surcharge rule entirely, yet its existing code reaches 100% branch coverage. What is the limitation?

options.text: Reachable code can still omit required business rules
Full branch coverage includes absent requirements
The omission makes coverage calculations undefined
Branch coverage measures stakeholder satisfaction

questions.explanation: Coverage measures the structure that exists. A missing business rule needs requirements-based evidence; neither coverage alone nor stakeholder satisfaction can be inferred from code reachability. Syllabus reference: FL-4.3.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team organizes exploratory testing around 60-minute charters. What should it retain for useful accountability?

options.text: A claim of complete requirements coverage
Observations, tested areas and a session debrief
A fixed sequence that forbids adapting to discoveries
The count of mouse clicks made

questions.explanation: Charters and recorded observations make exploration communicable. Click counts do not describe coverage, universal coverage claims are unsupported, and adapting to findings is central to exploration. Syllabus reference: FL-4.4.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester uses a list of common accessibility and validation conditions, choosing detailed inputs during execution. Which technique fits?

options.text: A formal decision table
Checklist-based testing
A fully specified execution script
Branch coverage analysis

questions.explanation: The list guides what to check while leaving detailed cases to judgment. A script prescribes steps more tightly; branches and decision tables derive from different coverage models. Syllabus reference: FL-4.4.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO valid styles for documenting acceptance criteria.

options.text: Private implementation guesses unrelated to needs
Scenario-oriented examples
Rule-oriented constraints
Unverifiable statements of enthusiasm

questions.explanation: Scenarios and rules can express evaluable behavior. Enthusiasm without observable conditions and irrelevant implementation guesses do not give dependable acceptance criteria. Syllabus reference: FL-4.5.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: An input has four specified equivalence partitions. A suite exercises representatives of three different partitions. What is its equivalence-partition coverage?
questions.explanation: Coverage is exercised partitions divided by total partitions: 3/4 × 100 = 75%. The number of values within each exercised partition does not alter this measure; the fourth partition remains uncovered. Syllabus reference: FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A temperature accepts integers 10–20 inclusive. Which set gives three-value BVA at both boundaries?
questions.explanation: Three-value BVA takes each boundary and both immediate neighbors: 9/10/11 and 19/20/21. Four points cover only two-value BVA; distant or exclusively valid points miss required neighboring values. Syllabus reference: FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: Rule: a member receives a discount regardless of coupon; a non-member receives it only with a valid coupon. Which TWO combinations receive a discount?

options.text: Non-member with no valid coupon
Member with no coupon
Non-member with a valid coupon
Non-member with an invalid coupon

questions.explanation: Membership alone grants the discount; a valid coupon grants it to a non-member. Both non-member distractors lack a valid coupon, so the specified rule denies the discount. Syllabus reference: FL-4.2.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: States are Draft, Submitted and Approved. Valid transitions are Draft→Submitted, Submitted→Draft and Submitted→Approved. Starting Draft, a test submits then approves. Which uncovered transition must another test exercise for full valid-transition coverage?

options.text: Return from Approved to Draft
Move from Draft directly to Approved
Move from Approved to Submitted
Return from Submitted to Draft

questions.explanation: Submit then approve covers two of the three listed transitions. The remaining valid transition is Submitted→Draft. The other transitions are not defined as valid in this model. Syllabus reference: FL-4.2.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: Criterion: after three consecutive failed logins, an account locks; a successful login before lock resets the count. Which sequence tests the reset behavior?

options.text: Fail, succeed, fail; account becomes locked
Fail, fail, succeed, fail; account remains unlocked
Succeed, fail, fail; account becomes locked
Fail, fail, fail; account remains unlocked

questions.explanation: The successful third attempt resets the count, so the final failure is the first of a new sequence. Three consecutive failures should lock; one or two failures after reset should not. Syllabus reference: FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: Which distribution best reflects the test pyramid?

options.text: A ban on testing user workflows
Many small checks and fewer broad end-to-end checks
The same number of checks at every scope
Few component checks and many broad end-to-end checks

questions.explanation: The pyramid encourages a broad base of small, fast checks and a smaller set of broad checks. It does not demand identical counts or eliminate end-to-end evidence. Syllabus reference: FL-5.1.6 (K1).

questions.prompt: An environment must be ready before system execution begins; an agreed defect threshold must be met before it finishes. How are these criteria classified?

options.text: Both are exit because they refer to quality
Environment readiness is entry; defect threshold is exit
Environment readiness is exit; defect threshold is entry
Both are entry because they refer to testing

questions.explanation: Entry conditions enable starting an activity; exit conditions enable completion. Their function, rather than the words “environment” or “defect,” determines the classification. Syllabus reference: FL-5.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A load test critiques throughput using technical measures. Which testing quadrant best fits?

options.text: Q1: technology-facing support for development
Q4: technology-facing product evaluation
Q2: business-facing support for development
Q3: business-facing product evaluation

questions.explanation: Load and technical performance evaluation belong in Q4. Q1 concerns development-supporting technical checks; Q2 acceptance examples support work; Q3 assesses business-facing product use. Syllabus reference: FL-5.1.7 (K2).

questions.prompt: A payment failure has greater assessed product risk than a cosmetic issue. How should that influence testing?

options.text: Treat the risk ranking as proof of a future failure
Delete every test outside the payment area
Use the same effort regardless of risk differences
Investigate payment behavior more thoroughly

questions.explanation: Risk analysis guides effort, techniques and scope. It need not eliminate all lower-risk checks, ignore differences or predict with certainty that a failure will occur. Syllabus reference: FL-5.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A remote release team includes engineers and business managers. How should test status be communicated?

options.text: Use a private conversation instead of an accessible record
Send unexplained logs and expect similar interpretation
Summarize implications and link technical detail
Omit blocked cases until test execution has finished

questions.explanation: Different audiences need different detail; shared summaries and linked evidence support understanding. Unexplained logs, private-only discussion and hidden blockers undermine informed decisions. Syllabus reference: FL-5.3.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A rerun uses updated data with the same build and test procedure and now passes. What configuration information is essential to interpret the change?

options.text: The number of unused accounts in a different release
The office location where the first report was written
The alphabetical ordering of tester names
The versions of both data sets

questions.explanation: Data changes can affect reproducibility and conclusions. Recording versions lets investigators compare conditions; irrelevant administrative or unrelated counts do not explain the changed outcome. Syllabus reference: FL-5.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Historical testing effort is 25% of development effort for comparable work. Development is estimated at 160 hours. Using that ratio, what is the testing estimate?

options.text: 120 hours
64 hours
40 hours
25 hours

questions.explanation: The ratio gives 0.25 × 160 = 40 hours. Twenty-five treats a percentage as hours; sixty-four uses the wrong ratio; 120 is the remaining share rather than testing effort. Syllabus reference: FL-5.1.4 (K3).
