questions.prompt: Risk priorities are Payment highest, Search medium, Profile lowest. Payment requires Account Setup first. No other dependencies apply. Which ordering honors risk and dependencies?

options.text: Payment, Account Setup, Search, Profile
Account Setup, Payment, Search, Profile
Profile, Search, Account Setup, Payment
Search, Profile, Payment, Account Setup

questions.explanation: Setup must precede Payment even though Payment has the highest risk. Once the prerequisite is met, Payment comes before medium and low risk. The other orders violate dependency or unnecessarily defer the highest risk. Syllabus reference: FL-5.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: A mobile crash occurs only for an offline session with a cached cart. Which defect-report precondition is most useful?

options.text: The reporter likes the application interface
The developer should rewrite the cache immediately
The team has tested another device in an unrelated release
Identify build, device, network mode and stored cart data

questions.explanation: These conditions help reproduce the particular crash. Opinion, a proposed fix and unrelated evidence do not establish the setup that triggers the observed failure. Syllabus reference: FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A tool flags unreachable code and coding-rule violations without executing the application. Which category fits?

options.text: Performance testing
Test execution
Service virtualization
Static analysis

questions.explanation: Static analysis inspects structured work products without running them. Performance and execution tools observe runtime behavior; virtualization supplies substitutes for dependencies rather than performs this analysis. Syllabus reference: FL-6.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which risk should be considered when adopting a record-and-playback interface tool?

options.text: The certainty that every recorded action detects a defect
The inability to automate any repeatable checks
The disappearance of all execution-time savings
Maintenance costs when screen layout and controls change

questions.explanation: Interface scripts can be fragile and require maintenance after changes. This is a risk to evaluate, not a claim that automation never saves time or that every action detects a defect. Syllabus reference: FL-6.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Select TWO typical test objectives.

options.text: Verify satisfaction of specified requirements
Validate suitability for stakeholder use
Prove that the product contains no defects
Set business profit targets for next year

questions.explanation: Verification and validation are testing objectives. Testing cannot prove absence of all defects; profit targets are business planning rather than evaluating work products. Syllabus reference: FL-1.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which practice fits a whole-team approach to quality?

options.text: Every team member must perform the same daily tasks
Testers help colleagues develop useful testing skills
Business representatives avoid acceptance discussions
Developers delegate all quality concerns to a separate team

questions.explanation: Sharing expertise helps the team contribute to quality. Delegating all quality, excluding business input or requiring identical duties contradicts complementary contributions. Syllabus reference: FL-1.5.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: A programmer misreads a rule, writes a wrong comparison, and an eligible customer is rejected. What is the observed rejection?

options.text: An error
A failure
A root cause
A defect

questions.explanation: The rejection is observed incorrect behavior, a failure. Misreading is the human error; the comparison is the defect; an underlying reason for the mistake would be a root cause. Syllabus reference: FL-1.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Most discovered defects are concentrated in two modules. Which testing response uses the clustering principle sensibly?

options.text: Attribute the defects to module size without investigation
Focus investigation there and assess remaining risks
Infer that the remaining modules are defect-free
Remove regression checks from the affected modules

questions.explanation: Clustering guides focused investigation but does not prove unexamined areas safe. Removing regression or reducing every cause to size is unsupported by the observation. Syllabus reference: FL-1.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Cases have been designed. The tester now prepares accounts, data and an execution sequence. Which activity is the main focus?

options.text: Test monitoring
Test analysis
Test implementation
Test completion

questions.explanation: Implementation prepares runnable testware and environments. Analysis identifies conditions, monitoring tracks progress, and completion consolidates finished work. Syllabus reference: FL-1.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Requirement-to-test links show that a high-risk requirement has no associated case. What does this expose?

options.text: A guarantee that adding one case will eliminate its risk
Missing planned coverage for that high-risk behavior
Proof that existing test results are incorrect
Proof that the implementation is defective

questions.explanation: Traceability can reveal missing planned coverage. The gap is not proof of a code defect or incorrect earlier results, and one case cannot guarantee removal of every associated risk. Syllabus reference: FL-1.4.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which task most directly belongs to the test-management role?

options.text: Prepare the detailed data for one test case
Derive individual boundary-value inputs
Coordinate resources and monitor test progress
Execute a specified API check

questions.explanation: Coordination and monitoring are management responsibilities. Input derivation, execution and detailed data preparation are technical testing activities, although one person can perform both roles. Syllabus reference: FL-1.4.5 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester examines an unexpected result and designs a follow-up to distinguish two possible explanations. Which skill is most directly demonstrated?

options.text: Personal blame attribution
Sales negotiation
Administrative invoice processing
Analytical thinking

questions.explanation: Designing evidence to distinguish explanations uses analytical reasoning. Commercial or administrative duties and blaming a person do not explain the investigative behavior. Syllabus reference: FL-1.5.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why establish objectives and an appropriate basis for each test level?

options.text: To ensure all levels find identical defects
To avoid reviewing development artifacts
To require all tests to run on production data
To focus evaluation on the purpose of its stage

questions.explanation: Objectives and a basis focus checks and expected results at each level. Levels need not find the same defect types, and neither reviews nor controlled test data are excluded. Syllabus reference: FL-2.1.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which approach collaboratively derives acceptance tests before implementing a user story?

options.text: Acceptance test-driven development
Acceptance coverage measurement
Defect trend monitoring
Exploratory session management

questions.explanation: ATDD uses agreed acceptance examples to guide implementation. Exploratory management organizes investigations; statement analysis evaluates structure; defect trends support monitoring. Syllabus reference: FL-2.1.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: A payroll application exchanges files with an external bank service. Tests check that interaction. Which level is the primary focus?

options.text: System integration testing
User acceptance testing
Component integration testing
Component testing

questions.explanation: Interactions between systems or external services are the focus of system integration. Lower levels target components; user acceptance checks readiness for stakeholder needs rather than this interface specifically. Syllabus reference: FL-2.2.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A repaired defect is checked with the inputs that originally triggered it. What is the primary purpose?

options.text: Confirmation that the specific failure no longer occurs
Replacement of checks for adverse effects elsewhere
Discovery of the developer's original reasoning mistake
Measurement of every branch in the system

questions.explanation: Confirmation testing evaluates the repaired behavior. Debugging investigates causes; branch measurement is structural coverage; regression remains needed for possible side effects. Syllabus reference: FL-2.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A retrospective compares promised improvement actions with results from the next iteration. Why is this useful?

options.text: Assess whether the change was effective
It replaces collecting test execution evidence
It certifies future iterations as defect-free
It imposes identical practices across different teams

questions.explanation: Reviewing effects supports evidence-based process improvement. It cannot certify future iterations, replace product testing or prescribe one process for all contexts. Syllabus reference: FL-2.1.6 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO ways DevOps can support testing.

options.text: Continuous deployment proves every requirement is correct
Pipeline tools eliminate the need for test design
Cross-functional collaboration reduces handover friction
Automated checks provide faster delivery feedback

questions.explanation: DevOps practices can speed feedback and improve collaboration. Deployment itself does not prove correctness, and useful automated checks still require thoughtful design. Syllabus reference: FL-2.1.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which item is suitable for a review-based static test?

options.text: A timing benchmark that runs the application
A proposed test case with expected results
An executed user session on a new binary
A live throughput experiment on a running service

questions.explanation: A test case can be reviewed as a work product, including its expectations. Throughput experiments, executed sessions and timing benchmarks run software and are dynamic activities. Syllabus reference: FL-3.1.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which review role records findings and agreed decisions during a meeting?

options.text: Scribe
Author
Moderator
Review manager

questions.explanation: The scribe documents findings and decisions. The moderator facilitates, the author owns the artifact, and management provides organizational support rather than this recording duty. Syllabus reference: FL-3.2.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: A review detects a missing rule; a runtime test reveals an incorrect output. Which distinction is accurate?

options.text: Both activities require executing the application
Static checks expose defects; dynamic checks expose failures
The missing rule can be found only through runtime coverage
The incorrect output is the human mistake itself

questions.explanation: Static review can directly reveal an omission. Dynamic execution produces an observed failure. Neither requires static review to run software, and the output is not itself a human error. Syllabus reference: FL-3.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: The review meeting has classified anomalies and agreed changes. Which activity closes the loop?

options.text: Replacing the artifact with execution logs
Starting a new review without tracking the changes
Fixing the work product and reporting follow-up results
Discarding findings after the meeting ends

questions.explanation: Fixing and reporting ensure findings lead to changes and tracked outcomes. Discarding or losing links prevents closure; execution logs are not a substitute for the reviewed artifact. Syllabus reference: FL-3.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester selects malformed dates because previous projects often mishandled them. Which family of techniques is the main basis?

options.text: Control-flow coverage
White-box
Experience-based
Black-box decision-table analysis

questions.explanation: The selection is driven by past defect experience, so it is experience-based error guessing. No structural model or explicitly analyzed condition table is given. Syllabus reference: FL-4.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A program has an if statement without an else, followed by a statement that runs for every input. Tests take only the true path. Why can statement coverage be complete while branch coverage is incomplete?

options.text: Branch coverage excludes conditional decisions
Statement coverage counts requirements rather than code
All statements can run without taking the false outcome
The false outcome adds an executable else statement by definition

questions.explanation: The true path can execute both the conditional body and following statement. The false outcome is still unexecuted even without an else body. Statement coverage concerns code, and decisions contribute branches. Syllabus reference: FL-4.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO appropriate interpretations of full structural coverage.

options.text: It establishes exhaustive coverage of input combinations
It can coexist with incorrect expected behavior
It provides evidence that modeled code items were exercised
It certifies implementation of omitted business rules

questions.explanation: Structural reachability is valuable but independent of whether results are correct. Missing rules and all combinations require evidence beyond the covered structure. Syllabus reference: FL-4.3.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester uses a fault checklist built from incidents: null input, duplicate submission and rounding errors. What is the main reason these cases were selected?

options.text: A complete table of all Boolean combinations
A requirement to execute every branch
A model of all states and transitions
Knowledge of plausible developer mistakes

questions.explanation: Incident-based fault ideas are error guessing. The stem does not describe branch coverage, a decision table or a state model as the derivation basis. Syllabus reference: FL-4.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why review and update a testing checklist after a new category of failures appears?

options.text: To keep its guidance relevant to current risks
To turn it into proof of exhaustive testing
To remove the need for observations during execution
To forbid testers from using judgment

questions.explanation: A checklist evolves with risks and experience. Updating it neither guarantees completeness nor removes judgment and recording of actual behavior. Syllabus reference: FL-4.4.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A user story states a requested feature but omits why the user needs it. What should the conversation clarify?

options.text: The exact database table names before discussing behavior
The tester's preferred automation framework
The total number of future regression scripts
The user's goal and the value of the capability

questions.explanation: Understanding user value helps judge desired behavior and examples. Implementation names, framework preferences and speculative script counts do not resolve the missing need. Syllabus reference: FL-4.5.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A form has three payment-method partitions and two delivery-method partitions. Every combination is feasible. What is the minimum number of cases to cover each partition of both inputs, without requiring combination coverage?
questions.explanation: Three cases can cover the three payment partitions and include both delivery partitions, for example P1/D1, P2/D2 and P3/D1. Two cannot cover three payment partitions; six covers all combinations, a stronger requirement than stated. Syllabus reference: FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A balance rule accepts amounts 100.00–200.00 inclusive, with resolution 0.01. Which pair checks the lower boundary using two-value BVA?
questions.explanation: The boundary is 100.00 and the closest point across it is 99.99 at the stated resolution. Interior neighbors apply to three-value analysis; one-unit jumps are not immediate neighbors. Syllabus reference: FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: Access requires authentication and either admin status or an active subscription. Which TWO cases are permitted?

options.text: Unauthenticated admin with active subscription
Authenticated non-admin without subscription
Authenticated non-admin with active subscription
Authenticated admin without subscription

questions.explanation: Authentication is mandatory. After it, either admin status or active subscription suffices. One distractor lacks authentication; the other satisfies neither of the alternative granting conditions. Syllabus reference: FL-4.2.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: A session model has transitions Anonymous→SignedIn on login, SignedIn→Anonymous on logout and SignedIn→Expired on timeout. Tests login and logout only. What is state coverage?
questions.explanation: Anonymous and SignedIn are visited, but Expired is not. The denominator is the three modeled states, not the executed events; transition coverage is a different metric even where values coincide. Syllabus reference: FL-4.2.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: Acceptance rules say cancellations before shipment return the full payment; cancellations after shipment are refused. Which example exposes an implementation that incorrectly refunds shipped orders?

options.text: Given Shipped, cancel; expect refusal and no refund
Given Shipped, cancel; expect a full refund
Given Unshipped, cancel; expect refusal
Given Unshipped, cancel; expect a full refund

questions.explanation: The correct case applies the negative rule to a shipped order. The valid unshipped case does not expose this defect; the other choices encode expectations contrary to the agreed rules. Syllabus reference: FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: Using a risk-rating model that multiplies likelihood by impact, what determines risk level?

options.text: Likelihood × impact
Requirement count × test count
Impact × number of developer comments
Likelihood × number of test scripts

questions.explanation: The stated model combines the chance rating and consequence rating. Script age, comment counts and IDs may be recorded but do not calculate risk level. Syllabus reference: FL-5.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: A plan states the test approach but omits people and environments needed. What is the practical consequence?

options.text: Resource feasibility and responsibilities remain unclear
Every planned test automatically becomes invalid
The approach no longer describes any testing activity
The test results become available without execution

questions.explanation: Plans need resources and responsibilities to support delivery. Missing them creates uncertainty but does not automatically invalidate all cases or manufacture execution evidence. Syllabus reference: FL-5.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Automated component checks support developers while code is being built. Which quadrant fits their primary role?

options.text: Q3: business-facing critique
Q4: technology-facing critique
Q1: technology-facing support
Q2: business-facing support

questions.explanation: Component checks supporting development belong in Q1. Q2 uses business-facing guidance, while Q3 and Q4 primarily critique the product from their respective perspectives. Syllabus reference: FL-5.1.7 (K2).

questions.prompt: A high-impact data-loss risk is identified. Which TWO responses can help address it?

options.text: Increase recovery testing and verify mitigation controls
Hide blocked recovery checks from the release report
Explicitly document residual risk for an informed acceptance decision
Assume the risk disappears after its first passing test

questions.explanation: Mitigation evidence and informed residual-risk acceptance are valid responses. One passing check cannot erase the risk, and concealing missing evidence prevents sound decisions. Syllabus reference: FL-5.2.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: How does a test completion report primarily differ from a progress report?

options.text: It replaces detailed defect records with personal judgments
It consolidates milestone outcomes and remaining risk
It is only a list of future execution steps
It must contain no testing results

questions.explanation: Completion reporting consolidates achieved results, deviations and remaining risk. It can reference detailed findings but is not a future procedure or an appraisal of people. Syllabus reference: FL-5.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A release baseline is used for testing. What should it identify?

options.text: A promise that no later changes will occur
The agreed versions of related product and test items
An unordered collection of whatever files are newest
Only the date of the next team meeting

questions.explanation: A baseline provides an identifiable consistent set of versions. “Newest” without control is not reproducible, and dates or promises do not define configuration items. Syllabus reference: FL-5.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team estimates 30 comparable cases remaining. Its observed execution rate is 6 cases per hour, with setup already complete. What is the extrapolated execution effort?

options.text: 24 hours
6 hours
5 hours
180 hours

questions.explanation: Effort is remaining cases divided by rate: 30/6=5 hours. Six repeats the rate, 24 subtracts quantities with different units, and 180 multiplies where division is needed. Syllabus reference: FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: Requirement priorities are R1 highest, R2 medium, R3 lowest. T1 checks R3, T2 checks R1 and T3 checks R2. There are no dependencies. Using requirements-based prioritization, what is the order?
questions.explanation: Order cases by their requirements’ priorities: the case for R1 is T2, then R2 is T3, then R3 is T1. Case numbers do not determine priority, and the absence of dependencies means the stated priority order can be applied directly. Syllabus reference: FL-5.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: A reproducible issue loses customer data but the report calls it “cosmetic.” Which report field should be corrected to reflect observed consequences?

options.text: Reporter name
Submission timestamp
Severity
Test-case identifier

questions.explanation: Severity describes impact, so data loss is inconsistent with a cosmetic classification. Identity, reference and time fields do not communicate the seriousness of the failure. Syllabus reference: FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: A team needs to organize cases, execution status and requirement coverage in one place. Which tool category is the best fit?

options.text: Static code analysis
Compiler optimization
Test management
Load generation

questions.explanation: Test-management tools support organizing and reporting testing evidence and links. Load tools exercise performance, analysis inspects code, and compiler optimization does not manage the test process. Syllabus reference: FL-6.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO risks of test automation.

options.text: Incorrect oracles can give misleading passing results
Repeated routine work can require less manual effort
Flaky dependencies can reduce trust in feedback
Checks can execute consistently under controlled conditions

questions.explanation: Wrong expectations and flaky dependencies undermine useful evidence. Consistent execution and less repetitive manual work are potential benefits rather than the requested risks. Syllabus reference: FL-6.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which activity is primarily quality assurance rather than product testing?

options.text: Measuring service response time under load
Reviewing a particular user story for contradictions
Improving the review process to prevent recurring omissions
Executing a checkout case and comparing the total

questions.explanation: Process improvement is QA-oriented prevention. Executing, measuring and reviewing specific work products are product evaluation activities, including static and dynamic testing. Syllabus reference: FL-1.2.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which behavior best supports shared quality responsibility?

options.text: Business representatives avoid clarifying examples
Collaborate on investigating failures and improving checks
Developers stop running checks once a tester joins
Testers conceal findings until the end of an iteration

questions.explanation: Joint investigation and improvement combine skills and support ownership. Abandoning checks, concealing evidence and avoiding clarification reduce the team's ability to address quality. Syllabus reference: FL-1.5.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: A team finds that repeated requirement mistakes stem from excluding domain experts from refinement. What does that exclusion represent in this investigation?

options.text: A root cause
A runtime failure
The expected output of a test
An executable defect

questions.explanation: The exclusion is an underlying reason for recurring mistakes. It is not an observed runtime failure, code flaw or expected result; addressing it can help prevent repetition. Syllabus reference: FL-1.2.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: A unchanged suite keeps passing, while recent incidents expose risks it never checked. Which response addresses tests wearing out?

options.text: Treat repeat passes as proof that incidents are unrelated
Refresh cases using evolving conditions
Rename existing passing cases without changing coverage
Remove the suite and stop regression testing

questions.explanation: Refreshing cases can reveal problems missed by unchanged checks. Renaming does not change evidence; passing old checks does not dismiss incidents, and useful regression still has value. Syllabus reference: FL-1.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A lead compares executed tests with the plan, then moves engineers to unblock high-risk cases. Which TWO activities are represented?

options.text: Test design
Test control
Test completion
Test monitoring

questions.explanation: Comparing actual progress with plans is monitoring; changing actions in response is control. The scenario does not derive new cases or consolidate a completed milestone. Syllabus reference: FL-1.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A project has a strict regulatory evidence requirement. How should that context affect its test process?

options.text: Remove documentation because execution is sufficient
Plan suitable traceability, records and review responsibilities
Treat tool selection as the sole compliance activity
Use the process from an unrelated informal prototype unchanged

questions.explanation: Context shapes evidence and responsibilities as well as execution. Copying an unsuitable approach, relying solely on tools or discarding records does not address the stated constraint. Syllabus reference: FL-1.4.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A defect is linked to its failing case, execution and original requirement. Which TWO uses do these links support?

options.text: Guaranteeing all other requirements pass
Automatically proving the root cause
Assessing which requirement is affected
Understanding the evidence behind the finding

questions.explanation: Links support impact and evidence assessment. They cannot by themselves diagnose causes or establish results for unrelated requirements. Syllabus reference: FL-1.4.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: A separate testing group finds defects but has little contact with developers and becomes a release bottleneck. What is the main drawback illustrated?

options.text: Developer checks are incompatible with independent testing
All testing must therefore be performed by authors
Organizational isolation can delay delivery
Independent perspectives cannot reveal new defects

questions.explanation: The issue is isolation and bottlenecking, a possible drawback of independence. Independent perspective can still be useful, and it can coexist with developer checks without forcing one universal staffing model. Syllabus reference: FL-1.5.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Which good practice helps prevent downstream defects during development?

options.text: Wait for release packaging before considering testability
Assign every level an identical test basis
Involve testers in reviews of requirements and designs
Use production incidents as the first quality feedback

questions.explanation: Early tester involvement can expose ambiguity and testability problems. Waiting for packaging or incidents loses early feedback; test bases and objectives differ by level. Syllabus reference: FL-2.1.2 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which sequence best describes the core TDD cycle?

options.text: Write a failing test, make it pass, then refactor
Measure defect density, then choose a supplier
Refactor, deploy, then write an unexecuted test
Complete all features, then select acceptance participants

questions.explanation: TDD starts with a failing component test, adds sufficient implementation, and refactors with checks preserved. The other sequences concern unrelated or delayed activities rather than the cycle. Syllabus reference: FL-2.1.3 (K1).

questions.prompt: Tests are derived from source branches and assert the computed results. Which description is accurate?

options.text: They cannot check behavior because structure was used
They use white-box derivation and can still check functional behavior
They belong to acceptance level solely because assertions exist
They are static because the source was consulted

questions.explanation: A structural basis makes derivation white-box, but execution and assertions can assess behavior. Source knowledge does not make execution static or determine the test level. Syllabus reference: FL-2.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: An old service is being retired, with data retained for future audit. What maintenance-testing concern is appropriate?

options.text: Verify the archival and retrieval arrangements
Rerun an unrelated interface test without impact analysis
Test only features added to the retired service next year
Assume retirement makes retained data irrelevant

questions.explanation: Retirement can require verification of archival access and retention. Future features, ignoring data or choosing unrelated checks do not address the stated operational change. Syllabus reference: FL-2.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A sequential project maps planned acceptance testing to stakeholder needs and system testing to system requirements. What benefit does that mapping provide?

options.text: Proof that execution can find every possible defect
An obligation to use identical cases at all levels
A requirement for testing to avoid early reviews
A suitable test basis and objectives at each level

questions.explanation: Mapping levels to corresponding work products supports focused planning and evaluation. It does not promise exhaustiveness, prohibit reviews or make different levels interchangeable. Syllabus reference: FL-2.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO statements consistent with shift left.

options.text: Review requirements before defects propagate into code
Eliminate all system testing once component tests exist
Move every acceptance decision before stakeholder examples are agreed
Design relevant checks earlier while retaining later evaluation

questions.explanation: Earlier suitable activities provide feedback sooner, while later evaluation remains important. Shift left neither eliminates system testing nor bypasses agreement on stakeholder expectations. Syllabus reference: FL-2.1.5 (K2).

questions.prompt: Frequent feedback on small increments most directly helps a team do what?

options.text: Replace confirmation testing after defect fixes
Adjust understanding when stakeholder needs change
Guarantee that the original requirements never evolve
Avoid communicating about completed behavior

questions.explanation: Frequent feedback helps detect changed or misunderstood needs. It does not freeze requirements, remove communication or provide confirmation of a code fix by itself. Syllabus reference: FL-3.2.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: Which review practice supports a constructive culture?

options.text: Reward reviewers for agreeing regardless of evidence
Use findings to rank individual authors publicly
Discuss defects in the work product using clear evidence
Prevent clarification questions to shorten the meeting

questions.explanation: Focusing on work-product evidence supports useful evaluation. Public ranking, pressured agreement and suppressed clarification undermine review goals and psychological safety. Syllabus reference: FL-3.2.5 (K1).

questions.prompt: A static analysis tool flags unreachable code before execution. What benefit can this provide?

options.text: Measured evidence of peak-load response time
Early detection of flaws in source structure
A guarantee that every flagged issue is a user-visible failure
Replacement of requirements-based testing

questions.explanation: Static analysis can detect structural issues before dynamic testing. It does not measure runtime load, guarantee user-visible consequences for every finding or replace requirements evidence. Syllabus reference: FL-3.1.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A team chooses the most formal review type, with defined roles, prescribed steps and collected review information. Which type best fits?

options.text: Author-led walkthrough
Inspection
Informal review
Exploratory session

questions.explanation: Inspection is the most formal review type. Informal reviews have fewer prescribed steps, walkthroughs are typically author-led, and exploratory sessions execute and investigate software rather than review an artifact this way. Syllabus reference: FL-3.2.4 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why combine specification-based and structure-based techniques?

options.text: They ensure each technique finds identical defects
They make experience-based investigation unusable
They expose different coverage gaps
They remove the need for expected outcomes

questions.explanation: Requirements coverage and structural reachability address different omissions. Combining them broadens evidence without guaranteeing identical findings, removing oracles or excluding experience-based work. Syllabus reference: FL-4.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: A suite reports 80% statement coverage. Which interpretation is justified?

options.text: Exactly 20% of decision outcomes were not taken
Exactly 20% of the product's defects remain
Some executable statements were not exercised
Exactly 20% of requirements are missing

questions.explanation: Statement coverage describes executed statements. It cannot be converted directly into requirements, branches or defect percentages; those need their own evidence. Syllabus reference: FL-4.3.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO accurate statements about branch coverage.

options.text: Full statement coverage necessarily includes full branch coverage
It measures exercised control-flow branches
Full branch coverage includes full statement coverage for the modeled structure
It measures the percentage of requirements accepted by users

questions.explanation: Branches concern control-flow choices, and covering all modeled branches also reaches their statements. The reverse implication fails; requirements acceptance is a different measure. Syllabus reference: FL-4.3.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A tester anticipates an off-by-one error after studying a team's recurring mistakes and adds a targeted case. What is the main technique?

options.text: Error-based execution scheduling
Formal review inspection
Error guessing
Configuration baselining

questions.explanation: A plausible fault based on experience motivates error guessing. Scheduling and baselining organize work and versions; inspection reviews a work product rather than derives this runtime case. Syllabus reference: FL-4.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: During exploratory testing, an unexpected save behavior is observed. What is an appropriate next step?

options.text: Declare complete coverage from the first session
Design a focused experiment and record what it reveals
Replace all observations with a count of button presses
Ignore it because it was absent from the initial charter

questions.explanation: Exploration adapts to observations while retaining evidence. Ignoring discoveries, overclaiming coverage or recording only clicks prevents useful learning and communication. Syllabus reference: FL-4.4.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: Criterion: “The screen should feel nice.” What is its main weakness as acceptance criteria?

options.text: It requires a specific implementation algorithm
It specifies a test framework too precisely
It contains too many measurable thresholds
It lacks an agreed observable basis for evaluation

questions.explanation: The phrase gives no shared observable expectation. The problem is ambiguity, rather than excessive detail or prescribed tools and implementation. Syllabus reference: FL-4.5.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A shipping result has four output partitions: domestic free, domestic paid, international paid and rejected address. Existing cases produce both domestic outputs and a rejected address. Which additional case closes the output-partition gap?

options.text: An international address producing rejection
An international address producing paid delivery
A domestic address producing free delivery
A domestic address producing paid delivery

questions.explanation: The suite has exercised three of the four specified output classes. An international paid-delivery outcome covers the remaining class. More examples of the already covered outputs do not close this partition gap. Syllabus reference: FL-4.2.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: Integer scores have partitions below 50, 50–79 and 80 or above. Which set covers two-value BVA at both boundaries?
questions.explanation: The adjacent cross-partition pairs are 49/50 and 79/80. Other sets skip a boundary or the closest value across it, so they do not provide the requested boundary coverage. Syllabus reference: FL-4.2.2 (K3).

questions.prompt: A fee table has two Boolean conditions, Premium and Express. Premium=false with Express=true is infeasible. How many feasible rules remain in the full decision table?
questions.explanation: Two Boolean conditions initially give four combinations. Excluding the one stated infeasible combination leaves three. Two counts too few, four fails to exclude it, and eight introduces another condition. Syllabus reference: FL-4.2.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: From Ready, send moves to Waiting; from Waiting, reply moves to Done. Cancel is invalid in Waiting and must leave the state unchanged. Which test correctly checks the invalid transition?

options.text: Send, then cancel; expect state Done
Start Ready, then cancel; expect state Waiting
Send, then cancel; expect rejection and state Waiting
Send, then inspect; expect the initial state Ready

questions.explanation: Cancel from Waiting is explicitly invalid, so rejection with unchanged state is the correct expectation. The other tests cover valid behavior or states without attempting an invalid event. Syllabus reference: FL-4.2.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: Criterion: only active members can reserve; an active member cannot have more than two concurrent reservations. Which case tests the count restriction independently of membership eligibility?

options.text: Active member with no reservations adds one; expect refusal
Inactive member with two reservations adds one; expect success
Active member with two reservations adds one; expect refusal
Inactive member with no reservations adds one; expect refusal

questions.explanation: An eligible active member already at the limit isolates the count restriction. Inactive cases involve membership, and refusing the eligible empty account or accepting an inactive one contradicts the rules. Syllabus reference: FL-4.5.3 (K3).

questions.prompt: Which is a metric useful for monitoring test progress?

options.text: Number of characters in the project name
Alphabetical rank of the test leader
Number of unused meeting rooms
Number of planned tests executed

questions.explanation: Executed tests compared with the plan can indicate progress, though results and risk context are also needed. Naming and unrelated administrative quantities do not measure test progress. Syllabus reference: FL-5.3.1 (K1).

questions.prompt: A completion criterion is unmet, but stakeholders consider releasing anyway. What is an appropriate response?

options.text: Delete evidence of the incomplete testing
Claim testing achieved its original objective unchanged
Report the deviation and residual risk for an explicit decision
Redefine the criterion silently to match current results

questions.explanation: Criteria support decisions rather than conceal uncertainty. Explicitly reporting deviations and risks permits an informed exception; silent changes and erased evidence misrepresent outcomes. Syllabus reference: FL-5.1.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: An agreed business-facing acceptance example guides implementation of a discount. Which quadrant best fits?

options.text: Q4: technology-facing product critique
Q1: technology-facing support for development
Q3: business-facing product critique
Q2: business-facing support for development

questions.explanation: The example guides work using business expectations, the purpose of Q2. Q1 concerns technical support, and Q3/Q4 primarily evaluate the finished product from different perspectives. Syllabus reference: FL-5.1.7 (K2).

questions.prompt: A supplier cannot deliver the test environment on schedule, while the product may leak confidential data. How are these risks classified?

options.text: Both are project because a deadline exists
Both are product because testing is involved
Environment delay is project; data leakage is product
Environment delay is product; data leakage is project

questions.explanation: The delay threatens project delivery; leakage threatens product quality. Context does not collapse these different consequences into one category. Syllabus reference: FL-5.2.2 (K2).

questions.prompt: A dashboard shows 95% of executed tests passed but omits blocked security tests. What should a status update add?

options.text: A claim that the displayed pass percentage establishes readiness
The same percentage with more decimal places
The coverage gap and its implications for release risk
Names of people assigned to the blocked cases

questions.explanation: The missing high-risk evidence changes interpretation of the pass percentage. Precision or ownership alone is insufficient; the gap and decision implications must be communicated. Syllabus reference: FL-5.3.3 (K2).

questions.prompt: Select TWO items that should be controlled for reproducible testing.

options.text: An unrelated application's popularity rating
The tester's lunch choice
The test-data version
The environment configuration

questions.explanation: Data and environment changes can alter observations, so their configuration belongs in reproducible evidence. Personal preferences and unrelated ratings do not define the test conditions. Syllabus reference: FL-5.4.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: For a three-point estimate, use standard deviation SD=(P−O)/6. Optimistic effort is 6 days and pessimistic effort is 18 days. What is SD?

options.text: 3 days
2 days
6 days
12 days

questions.explanation: Substitute the bounds into the specified uncertainty formula: (18−6)/6=12/6=2 days. Twelve is the range before division; six is the optimistic input; neither is the standard deviation. This measure describes estimation uncertainty, not the expected effort. Syllabus reference: FL-5.1.4 (K3).

questions.prompt: T1 covers A,B; T2 covers A,B,C,D; T3 covers E,F,G. No dependencies apply. Use coverage-based prioritization by total items covered, without recalculating additional coverage. What is the order?
questions.explanation: Total coverage counts are four for T2, three for T3 and two for T1. Descending totals give T2,T3,T1. The question explicitly asks for total coverage, so overlapping items are not removed after selecting a test. Syllabus reference: FL-5.1.5 (K3).

questions.prompt: A reproducible data-loss issue has severe impact, but a documented workaround permits the release owner to schedule its fix later. Which report classification reflects impact separately from agreed urgency?

options.text: Low severity because the fix is scheduled later
Omit impact because a workaround has been approved
High severity with lower fix priority
High urgency solely because the title sounds serious

questions.explanation: Severity records the serious consequence of data loss; priority records the agreed urgency of remediation. A workaround can affect scheduling without making the underlying impact low. A title cannot establish urgency, and impact should remain documented. Syllabus reference: FL-5.5.1 (K3).

questions.prompt: An unavailable payment gateway blocks tests. A tool supplies configurable responses in its place. What support is being used?

options.text: Defect trend reporting
Static analysis
Statement coverage measurement
Service virtualization

questions.explanation: Virtualization substitutes controlled behavior for a dependency. Static analysis inspects artifacts, coverage measures executed structure, and trends summarize findings rather than simulate the gateway. Syllabus reference: FL-6.1.1 (K2).

questions.prompt: Why run a pilot before adopting an automation tool widely?

options.text: Avoid involving the people who will maintain checks
Conclude that manual activities should be automated
Evaluate integration, maintenance and useful feedback in context
Certify maintenance-free scripts for later versions

questions.explanation: A pilot supplies evidence about fit, costs and value. It cannot guarantee maintenance-free scripts, and excluding maintainers or assuming universal automation undermines the evaluation. Syllabus reference: FL-6.2.1 (K1).
